intro: A jar of milkweed leaves sits by a classroom window. In a month, five tiny eggs become five orange butterflies that fly off toward Mexico. Near Braidwood, a hammer taps a rust-colored rock, and it splits open on an animal that has been dead for 300 million years. Both are stories about life: how it begins, how it grows, how it passes on its traits, and how it ends.

Follow the life cycles of frogs, butterflies, beans and oaks. Find out why you look like your parents but not exactly like your brother or sister. See how a heart, a root, an eye and a shell each do a job that keeps a living thing alive. Then watch what happens when a pond dries up or a prairie becomes a farm.

By the end, you will be able to explain what a trait is and where it comes from, how a structure helps a plant or animal survive, how your senses reach your brain, and what a fossil in an Illinois rock can tell us about a world that is gone.
bigQuestion: How do living things grow, pass on their traits and survive in a changing world?

timeline.t: Robert Hooke looks at thin slices of cork through a microscope and names the tiny boxes he sees 'cells'
Nicolas Steno argues that rock layers pile up over time and that fossils are the remains of once-living things
Maria Sibylla Merian publishes her paintings of caterpillars, chrysalises and the butterflies they become
Gregor Mendel reports his pea-plant experiments showing that traits pass to offspring in predictable patterns
The last passenger pigeon, once among the most common birds in North America, dies in a zoo; the kind is extinct
Francis Tully splits open a Mazon Creek concretion near Braidwood and finds the first Tully monster
Field Museum scientist Eugene Richardson names the fossil Tullimonstrum
Illinois names the monarch its state insect; the same year, the monarchs' winter home in Mexico's mountains is found
The Tully monster becomes the Illinois state fossil
Bison return to the Illinois prairie at Nachusa Grasslands, more than 150 years after they were gone from the state

words.d: the stages a living thing goes through: birth, growth, reproduction and death
a big change in body shape as a young animal becomes an adult
a feature of a living thing, such as eye color or leaf shape
passed from parents to their young
the differences among members of one family or one kind of living thing
everything around a living thing: light, water, food, weather and other living things
a trait that helps a living thing survive or reproduce better than others of its kind
a part of a living thing that has a shape and a job
thin threads in the body that carry signals to and from the brain
the layer at the back of the eye that turns light into signals for the brain
the remains or trace of a living thing from long ago, preserved in rock
no longer alive anywhere on Earth

test.q: Which stage comes right after the caterpillar stage in a monarch's life cycle?
test.why: The order is egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, adult. A tadpole is a young frog, not a butterfly.

test.q: A tadpole breathes with gills. An adult frog breathes with lungs. What is the big change between them called?
test.why: Metamorphosis is the change of body form from a young animal to an adult.

choices: A dog's weight after a big meal
test.why: Fur color is passed from parents. A scar, a trick and a full belly come from things that happen during life.

test.q: Two bean plants from the same pod look different after a week in different places. The best explanation is:
test.why: Seeds from one pod share parents. Light, water and other parts of the environment changed how they grew.

test.q: Why is variation among brothers and sisters expected?
choices: They are born in different years
Each gets its own mix of traits from both parents
Only one of them inherits traits
test.why: Each child gets traits from both parents, and the mix is a little different every time.

test.q: A woodpecker with a stronger beak finds more food in winter. Over many generations, what would you predict?
test.why: Birds with the advantage survive and have young, and the young often inherit the stronger beak.

test.q: Why are many male birds brightly colored?
choices: Bright colors hide them from hawks
Females tend to choose bright males, so the trait is passed on
test.why: Bright males win more mates and have more young. That is sexual selection.

test.q: Which structure helps a plant take in water?
test.why: Roots reach into the soil and take in water. Petals attract insects, thorns defend, and leaves catch light.

choices: Turns light into signals for the brain
test.why: The retina is the layer at the back of the eye packed with cells that change light into signals.

test.q: A loud bang makes you jump. Which came first?
choices: Your ears sent a signal to your brain
test.why: The sense comes first. Ears send the signal along nerves, the brain decides, and then the muscles move.

test.q: Which is a benefit of living in a group?
test.why: More eyes mean danger is spotted sooner. Food still has to be shared, and sickness can spread faster.

test.q: A river floods a field for a whole summer. What can happen to the animals there?
choices: Some survive, some move, some die
test.why: When the environment changes, the result depends on each animal's traits: survive, move or die.

test.q: What is needed for a dead animal to become a fossil?
choices: It must be buried quickly in mud or sand
test.why: Quick burial keeps scavengers and oxygen away, so the remains last long enough to turn to stone.

test.q: Fossil corals are found across Illinois. Scientists infer that:
choices: Illinois was once under a shallow sea
test.why: Corals live in the sea. Their fossils in Illinois rock show a sea once covered the state.

test.q: The Tully monster is extinct. What does that mean?
choices: It only comes out at night
test.why: Extinct means no living members of that kind are left anywhere on Earth.

write.prompt: Choose one living thing from this unit: a monarch, a frog, an oak, a heron, or the Tully monster. Make a claim about one of its structures or traits and how it helps the living thing survive, grow or reproduce. Support your claim with evidence from the lessons and explain your reasoning.
tips: Claim: name the structure or trait and say what job it does, in one sentence.
Evidence: use at least two facts from the readings, the data tables or the fossil story.
Reasoning: explain how each piece of evidence shows the structure helps with survival, growth or reproduction.
The other side: describe one way the same structure could be a cost, and explain why the benefit still wins.
